implementation_notes: The language's own method is the filtering mechanism: Array.prototype.filter constructs a shallow copy of the array containing only the elements for which the callback returns truthy, so the criterion is simply a function value and the container-typed result is a method returning a new instance of the same class - filtered(keep) { return new ThreatAwareSystem(this.id, this.threats.filter(keep)); }. Criteria are ordinary functions or arrows and compose with && or by wrapping (const both = t => isRootkit(t) && recent(t)). This is the default form: synchronous, eager, index-aware (the callback receives element, index and the array) and identical in browsers, Node and workers; reach for the iterator-helper variant when a chain would materialise too many intermediate arrays.
pitfalls: The callback's extra arguments are a trap: passing a function by name (filter(parseInt), filter(Math.max), filter isAvailable.bind(obj)) silently receives the index as the second argument.

filter skips holes in sparse arrays and is generic over length plus integer keys, so it works on array-likes but silently reads whatever 'length' says; obj.filter(...) throws because the method lives on Array.prototype.
Each filter call builds a new array, so filtered(a).filtered(b).filtered(c) copies the surviving elements three times - compose predicates instead.
Mutating the array inside the predicate has unspecified reach: elements already visited are not re-checked, so the result depends on visit order.

variants.name: Lazy iterator filtering with Iterator.prototype.filter
variants.implementation_notes: Iterator helpers (Baseline 2025) move filtering onto iterators: Iterator.prototype.filter returns a new iterator helper that yields only the elements for which the callback is truthy, and consumes the underlying iterator only when next() is called. That makes the criterion a composable value over any iterable - generators, map/Set iterators, streams of records - and avoids the intermediate arrays an eager chain builds, which is the difference that matters for large or unbounded sources. Its documented advantage over array methods is exactly this laziness, so prefer it for pipelines; keep the array variant where the result must be an array or the target runtime predates the feature.
pitfalls: Iterator helpers are single-use: once an iterator helper is consumed (or partially consumed) it cannot be re-traversed, so a stored 'filtered view' must be re-created from the source each time.
Laziness moves errors to the consumer: a throwing predicate fails during iteration, not where the pipeline was built, and a pipeline that is never consumed never runs at all.
Mixing array and iterator APIs (Array.from(iter), spread) re-introduces the eager materialisation the helpers were chosen to avoid.
